hints: Trace the two different routes from the gaseous ions $\text{Fe}^{2+}(\text{g}) + \text{O}^{2-}(\text{g})$ and from $\text{Fe}(\text{s}) + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{O}_{2}(\text{g})$ down to $\text{FeO}(\text{s})$, then link them with the enthalpy of formation.

List every step on the upward route with its sign, remembering to halve the $\text{O}=\text{O}$ bond energy and to add both ionisation energies of Fe and both electron affinities of O from the Data Booklet.
walkthrough:
See the cycle as Hess's law in disguise**
Think of $\Delta H_{latt}$ as the big downward arrow on the right, from $\text{Fe}^{2+}(\text{g}) + \text{O}^{2-}(\text{g})$ to $\text{FeO}(\text{s})$. The left hand staircase plus the formation arrow $-272 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ gives you the other route to the same product. By Hess's law the sum round the loop is zero, so formation equals all the up steps plus lattice.

Collect the five up steps correctly**
From the diagram and Data Booklet: $\text{Fe}(\text{s}) \rightarrow \text{Fe}(\text{g})$ is $+416$, $\tfrac{1}{2}\text{O}_{2} \rightarrow \text{O}$ is $\tfrac{1}{2}(+496) = +248$, $\text{Fe} \rightarrow \text{Fe}^{2+}$ is $762 + 1560$, $\text{O} \rightarrow \text{O}^{2-}$ is $-141 + 798$. Add them: $416 + 248 + 762 + 1560 - 141 + 798 = +3643 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Solve for lattice**
$$-272 = +3643 + \Delta H_{latt}$$
$$\Delta H_{latt} = -272 - 3643 = -3915 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$
The large negative value makes sense because oppositely charged doubly charged ions attract very strongly when the lattice forms.

Final answer: $\Delta H_{f} = \Delta H_{at}(\text{Fe}) + \tfrac{1}{2}\Delta H_{at}(\text{O}_{2}) + IE_{1} + IE_{2} + EA_{1} + EA_{2} + \Delta H_{latt}$
$-272 = (+416) + \tfrac{1}{2}(+496) + (+762) + (+1560) + (-141) + (+798) + \Delta H_{latt}$
$\Delta H_{latt}\text{FeO}(\text{s}) = -3915 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

hints: Count how many of the 20 Fe atoms are $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ and how many are $\text{Fe}^{3+}$, then work out the total positive charge that the $x$ oxide ions must balance.
walkthrough:
Balance charge, not atoms**
A solid must be electrically neutral. Out of 20 Fe atoms, $90\%$ are $\text{Fe}^{2+}$: $0.9 \times 20 = 18$ $\text{Fe}^{2+}$, and $10\%$ are $\text{Fe}^{3+}$: $0.1 \times 20 = 2$ $\text{Fe}^{3+}$. Total positive charge is $18(2+) + 2(3+) = 36 + 6 = 42+$. Each $\text{O}^{2-}$ provides $2-$, so $$20(+2.1 \text{ average}) - 2x = 0$$
$$x = 21$$
Final answer: Total positive charge $= 18(+2) + 2(+3) = +42$, so $2x = 42$, $x = 21$. Formula is $\text{Fe}_{20}\text{O}_{21}$.

hints: Compare the charges on the ions in FeO and CaO, then compare the sizes of $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ and $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ using their positions in the Periodic Table.
Link a smaller ionic radius at the same charge to the strength of attraction between oppositely charged ions in the lattice.
walkthrough:
Keep charge constant, focus on size**
Both solids are $\text{M}^{2+}\text{O}^{2-}$ with the same charges, so the difference must come from ionic size. $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ is in Group 2 Period 4, $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ is a Period 4 transition metal ion with more protons pulling the same shell in. $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ is noticeably smaller.

Connect size to lattice strength**
Lattice energy depends on $\frac{q+ q-}{r+ + r-}$. With the same $2+$ and $2-$ charges but a smaller $r+$, the ions can approach more closely. The electrostatic attraction between $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ and $\text{O}^{2-}$ is stronger, more energy is released when the lattice forms, so $\Delta H_{latt}$ is more negative for FeO.

Final answer: $\Delta H_{latt}$ of FeO is more exothermic / more negative than that of CaO.
$\text{Fe}^{2+}$ is smaller than $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ so has higher charge density, giving stronger attraction to $\text{O}^{2-}$ and stronger ionic bonding.

hints: Assign the oxidation number of Fe on the left in FeO and on the right in Fe and in $\text{Fe}_{3}\text{O}_{4}$, remembering $\text{Fe}_{3}\text{O}_{4}$ contains one $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ and two $\text{Fe}^{3+}$.
walkthrough:
Spot the same element going both ways**
In $4\text{FeO}$, all Fe is $+2$. On the right, Fe metal is $0$, while $\text{Fe}_{3}\text{O}_{4}$ contains $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ and $\text{Fe}^{3+}$. So some $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ gains electrons to become $0$ (reduction) and other $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ loses electrons to become $+3$ (oxidation). One starting oxidation state both increases and decreases, which is exactly what disproportionation means.

Final answer: $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ is reduced to Fe, oxidation number $+2 \rightarrow 0$, and $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ is also oxidised to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$, oxidation number $+2 \rightarrow +3$. Same species both oxidised and reduced, so disproportionation.

hints: Decide which ion can reach the positive anode in molten $\text{Fe}_{3}\text{O}_{4}$ and remember oxidation with loss of electrons produces $\text{O}_{2}$ gas.
walkthrough:
Oxidation happens at the anode**
In the melt the only negative ion is $\text{O}^{2-}$. It is attracted to the positive anode, loses electrons and forms oxygen gas. Balance O then charge: $$2\text{O}^{2-} \rightarrow \text{O}_{2} + 4\text{e}^{-}$$

hints: Calculate total charge from $Q = It$ with time in seconds, then convert to moles of electrons using $F = 96500 \text{ C mol}^{-1}$.
Combine the cathode processes for one $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ needing $2\text{e}^{-}$ and two $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ needing $3\text{e}^{-}$ each to find electrons per 3 Fe atoms formed.
Convert your moles of Fe to mass using $A_{r} = 55.8$ and give the answer to at least 3 significant figures.
walkthrough:
Turn current and time into moles of electrons**
Charge is current times time in seconds: $$Q = It = 50 \times (6 \times 60 \times 60) = 1.08 \times 10^{6} \text{ C}$$
One mole of electrons carries $96500 \text{ C}$, so $$n(\text{e}^{-}) = \frac{1.08 \times 10^{6}}{96500} = 11.19 \text{ mol}$$

Work out electrons per Fe atom**
You are told one $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ and two $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ discharge together: $\text{Fe}^{2+} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Fe}$ and each $\text{Fe}^{3+} + 3\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Fe}$. Altogether: $$\text{Fe}^{2+} + 2\text{Fe}^{3+} + 8\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow 3\text{Fe}$$
So $8$ mol electrons make $3$ mol Fe. $$n(\text{Fe}) = \frac{3}{8} \times 11.19 = 4.20 \text{ mol}$$

Convert to mass**
$$m = n \times A_{r} = 4.20 \times 55.8 = 234 \text{ g}$$
This is the maximum theoretical mass if every electron goes to making iron.

Final answer: $Q = It = 50 \times 6 \times 3600 = 1.08 \times 10^{6} \text{ C}$
$n(\text{e}^{-}) = 1.08 \times 10^{6} / 96500 = 11.2 \text{ mol}$
$\text{Fe}^{2+} + 2\text{Fe}^{3+} + 8\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow 3\text{Fe}$, so $n(\text{Fe}) = 3/8 \times 11.2 = 4.20 \text{ mol}$
mass $= 4.20 \times 55.8 = 234 \text{ g}$ (234.2 g)

hints: Think about what makes a phone or electric car battery useful compared with a large lead acid battery, focusing on size, mass or voltage.
walkthrough:
Why lithium wins for portable power**
Lithium is the lightest metal and gives a very positive cell voltage. That means you can store a lot of energy in a very small, light package that can be recharged many times, ideal for phones, laptops and electric vehicles.
Final answer: Small / compact size or low mass / light or high voltage / high energy density.

hints: Use the cathode half equation $\text{Li}^{+} + \text{FePO}_{4} + \text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{LiFePO}_{4}$ and assign oxidation numbers to Li and Fe on each side, remembering $\text{PO}_{4}^{3-}$ is unchanged.
walkthrough:
Let phosphate do the bookkeeping**
In $\text{FePO}_{4}$, $\text{PO}_{4}$ is $3-$, so Fe must be $3+$ to balance. In $\text{LiFePO}_{4}$, $\text{Li}^{+}$ plus $\text{PO}_{4}^{3-}$ leaves $2+$ for Fe, so Fe is $2+$. $\text{Li}^{+}$ stays $+1$ throughout. At the cathode electrons are gained, and it is Fe that is reduced from $+3$ to $+2$.
Final answer: Lithium: from $+1$ to $+1$ (no change). Iron: from $+3$ to $+2$.

hints: Add the given anode and cathode half equations for discharging and cancel the species that appear on both sides ($\text{Li}^{+}$ and $\text{e}^{-}$).
walkthrough:
Add and cancel**
Anode: $\text{LiC}_{6} \rightarrow 6\text{C} + \text{Li}^{+} + \text{e}^{-}$. Cathode: $\text{Li}^{+} + \text{FePO}_{4} + \text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{LiFePO}_{4}$. Adding gives $\text{LiC}_{6} + \text{Li}^{+} + \text{FePO}_{4} + \text{e}^{-} \rightarrow 6\text{C} + \text{Li}^{+} + \text{e}^{-} + \text{LiFePO}_{4}$. Cancel $\text{Li}^{+}$ and $\text{e}^{-}$ to leave: $$\text{LiC}_{6} + \text{FePO}_{4} \rightarrow \text{LiFePO}_{4} + 6\text{C}$$
